paragraphs: The UN General Assembly voted to replace the traditional Mercator world map with the Equal Earth map to show Africa’s true size.
Proposed by Togo and supported by 164 nations, the non-binding resolution aims to influence education and governments worldwide.

Critics argue the Mercator map distorts landmasses by making equatorial regions, such as Africa, look much smaller than countries near the poles, like Greenland or Alaska. Cartographer Clancy Wilmott explains that neither map is real; the Mercator projection was created for navigation, while equal-area projections accurately maintain geographic proportions.

The United States was the only nation to vote against the resolution and claimed it is part of an ideological movement. However, experts view this change as a practical step toward better representing global issues like aid, health, and development.

paragraphs: The UN voted to change the traditional world map to a new one called the Equal Earth map. This new map shows the real size of Africa and countries near the equator.

The old Mercator map was made for ocean travel, so it makes places near the poles, like Greenland, look much bigger than they really are. Most countries supported the non-binding resolution, but the United States voted against it. They called the idea political.
Experts say that no flat map is perfect, but the new map helps people see the true size of continents. This change will help schools and governments understand world issues much better.

paragraphs: The UN vote for a new world map. The old map makes Africa look very small, and Greenland look very big.

The new map shows the true size of all continents and countries. Most countries like the new map, but the USA vote no. The USA says that this idea is only about politics. Map experts say that the old map is good for ships. But the new map is better for schools and learning. It helps people see the world correctly. People will better understand some problems in the world.
